Profiling Rust code with flamegraphs

Anika Rao · 5 October 2026 · 6 min read

A flamegraph shows where a program spends its time, one box for every function on the stack, as wide as the time it took. Reading one takes a little practice, but after a few minutes the wide plateaus jump out at you and the narrow spikes stop being distracting.

Recording a profile #

To record a profile, build the program in release mode with debug symbols and run it under perf with call graphs turned on.

fn main() { let map = build_map_once(); serve(&map); }
  1. Build with --release.
  2. Run under perf record -g.
  3. Fold the stacks and draw the graph.

Reading the graph

The first thing to look for is a plateau that should not be there, a function that you expected to be cheap taking a quarter of the width. In our case it was the hash function of a map that was rebuilt for every request instead of once at start-up.

Moving the map into a static that is built lazily cut the time for a request from eleven milliseconds to four.

Other views

Flamegraphs are not the only view worth having, and a flat profile sorted by self time still answers some questions faster.

Self time
The time spent in the function itself.
Total time
The time spent in it and everything it calls.

The second profile, after the fix, has no plateau at all: the time is spread across parsing, the database and writing the answer.
